subject: Cooking
title: Celiac Disease: When Gluten Attacks
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Celiac Disease: When Gluten Attacks.

hook.text: For 1% of the global population, eating a single slice of bread triggers an autoimmune war inside their gut.

buildup.text: In celiac disease, the immune system mistakes gluten fragments for invaders and attacks the intestinal lining.

discovery.text: This destroys villi — the finger-like projections that absorb nutrients — leading to malnutrition despite eating enough.

twist.text: Celiac was described in 100 AD by the Greek physician Aretaeus — but wasn't linked to gluten until 1952.

climax.text: Dutch pediatrician Willem Dicke noticed celiac children improved during WWII bread shortages — proving the link.

punchline.text: A wartime bread shortage solved a 2,000-year medical mystery.

quiz.question: Who linked celiac disease to gluten during WWII bread shortages?

details.summary: Celiac disease is an autoimmune disorder where gluten triggers the immune system to attack the small intestine's villi, destroying nutrient absorption capacity. It affects about one percent of the population, and even trace amounts of gluten cause damage.
details.whyItMatters: Celiac disease transforms bread from life-sustaining staple to genuine threat. Understanding it separates a serious medical condition from the broader gluten-free trend.
takeaways: Immune system attacks intestinal villi when gluten is consumed
Affects approximately one percent of the global population
Even trace gluten causes intestinal damage in celiac patients

faq.question: How is celiac disease different from gluten sensitivity?
faq.answer: Celiac disease causes measurable autoimmune destruction of intestinal villi, confirmed by blood antibody tests and biopsy. Non-celiac gluten sensitivity causes symptoms but no detectable intestinal damage or antibodies.

faq.question: Why has celiac disease diagnosis increased so dramatically?
faq.answer: Better diagnostic tools catch cases that were previously missed. Blood antibody screening is now routine. Awareness has increased, prompting more people to get tested. Some researchers also theorize that changes in wheat breeding but this connection remains debated and unproven.
